profile.bio: Charlotte plans, made more social. Find events, see who's going, meet your people. Yard is in the works.

posts.title: A city feels smaller when you know someone there

slides.headline: New city. Same question.
slides.body: What should we do this weekend?

slides.headline: And the follow-up…
slides.body: Who’s going with me?

slides.headline: We’re building Yard for that.
slides.body: Find events around Charlotte and see where your friends are headed.

slides.headline: More plans. More familiar faces.
slides.body: Yard is in the works. We’ll share the journey here.

posts.caption: Moving somewhere new can make even a good weekend feel like a blank page. We’re building Yard to bring local plans and your people a little closer together, starting in Charlotte. Still a work in progress; glad you’re here for it.

posts.title: What is Yard?

slides.headline: Yard is a social way to make plans.
slides.body: We’re bringing event discovery and your friend plans together.

slides.headline: Find something happening.
slides.body: Browse events by day, interests, time and distance.

slides.headline: See where friends are going.
slides.body: Choose a plan and make it easier to show up together.

slides.headline: Meet your people out there.
slides.body: Yard is being built for Charlotte, one good plan at a time.

posts.caption: A useful plan has two parts: something worth doing and someone you’d like to do it with. Yard brings those pieces into one place. We’re building now, with Charlotte first.
posts.cta: Save this if that sounds like your kind of app.

posts.title: Your plans should feel like yours

slides.headline: Not every maybe is an announcement.
slides.body: Sometimes you’re just saving an idea for later.

slides.headline: Interested stays private.
slides.body: Yard’s save-for-later plan is visible only to you.

slides.headline: Going is different.
slides.body: When you commit, your friends and fellow attendees can see you’re going.

slides.headline: Clear choices. No guessing.
slides.body: We’re building privacy into the way plans work.

posts.caption: A small but important product decision: saving an event is just for you. Going is the commitment you choose to share with friends and other attendees. We’re designing Yard so each plan state is clear about who can see it.
posts.cta: What makes a social app feel comfortable to you?

posts.title: Making friends after college takes a little intention

slides.headline: Friendship needs a second hello.
slides.body: The first conversation is a start, not a whole friendship.

slides.headline: Make the invite specific.
slides.body: Try: “Want to get coffee next Tuesday?” A day and an idea make it easier to answer.

slides.headline: Choose something you’d do anyway.
slides.body: A walk, a class, a low-key meal. Keep the first plan easy to say yes to.

slides.headline: Then follow up.
slides.body: “I had a good time. Let’s do it again.” Simple counts.

posts.caption: After school, friendship can take more intention than it used to. A small, specific invitation is a kind place to start: one activity, one day, no big production. Save this for the next time you think, “We should hang out sometime.”
posts.cta: Save this for your next “we should hang out” moment.

posts.title: Three tiny habits for a new city

slides.headline: New city? Start smaller than a whole new life.
slides.body: You don’t need a perfect routine to feel more at home.

slides.headline: Pick one weekly anchor.
slides.body: A walk after work, a library hour, a regular class—something you can return to.

slides.headline: Learn one name at a time.
slides.body: Say hi to the person you keep seeing. Familiarity can start with a hello.

slides.headline: Leave room for a second visit.
slides.body: You don’t have to decide if it’s “your place” after one try.

posts.caption: Getting to know a new city doesn’t have to mean filling every night. Try one small repeatable thing, learn a name, and give a place more than one chance. Keep what feels good; leave what doesn’t.
posts.cta: What’s one little thing that helped a place feel familiar?

posts.title: The group chat has 47 messages and no plan

slides.headline: Skip “What does everyone want to do?”
slides.body: Open-ended questions are hard to answer when everyone’s busy.

slides.headline: Offer two real options.
slides.body: “Walk Saturday morning or dinner Sunday?” is easier to react to.

slides.headline: Add the useful details.
slides.body: Include a time, a rough cost if you know it, and where to meet.

slides.headline: Let a no be easy.
slides.body: “No worries if neither works” keeps the invite warm.

posts.caption: A little structure can get a plan unstuck: two options, a day, and the details people need to decide. No guilt, no 47-message poll. Send the invite, then let everyone answer honestly.
posts.cta: Copy the two-option trick into your next group chat.

posts.title: A good weekend plan can be very small

slides.headline: No big itinerary required.
slides.body: A nice weekend can have one easy thing in it.

slides.headline: Try a one-hour plan.
slides.body: Coffee and a walk. A market lap. A catch-up on a park bench.

slides.headline: Give it a clear start and finish.
slides.body: “Meet at 10, head out by 11” can feel easier to fit in.

slides.headline: Small plans still count.
slides.body: You made time for someone. That’s a good use of an hour.

posts.caption: When everyone’s tired, “let’s do something all day” can be a tough sell. Try one hour, one simple activity, and a clear end time. You can always keep hanging out if you’re both having a good time.
posts.cta: Send this to someone you’d like to see for an hour.

posts.title: Let your interests do the introducing

slides.headline: Not sure what to talk about? Start with the thing.
slides.body: A shared interest gives a first conversation somewhere to go.

slides.headline: Ask one open question.
slides.body: “How did you get into that?” is better than a rapid-fire interview.

slides.headline: Trade one recommendation each.
slides.body: A book, a trail, a recipe, a beginner class—keep it easy.

slides.headline: Make the next hello natural.
slides.body: “If you go again, let me know” leaves the door open.

posts.caption: A shared interest can take some pressure off meeting someone new. Ask what they enjoy about it, swap one recommendation, and let the conversation breathe. You don’t need to turn every nice chat into a new best friend.
posts.cta: What interest has introduced you to someone new?

posts.title: The text after you meet someone new

slides.headline: Liked talking to them? Say so.
slides.body: A kind follow-up doesn’t need a perfect opening.

slides.headline: Name the moment you shared.
slides.body: “It was fun talking about your pottery class.”

slides.headline: Offer one low-pressure next step.
slides.body: “Want to grab coffee next week?”

slides.headline: Leave room for their answer.
slides.body: Send it once. A warm invite is enough.

posts.caption:
The post-hangout text can be simple: “I liked talking with you about [thing]. Want to [easy activity] next week?” Be specific, be kind, and let the other person choose.

A tiny note from Yard: find your people.

reels.title: Three small ways to feel less new in a new city

timestampedScript.voiceover: Pick one place you’d happily go back to.
Learn one name. No need to collect a whole new friend group in a week.
Make one easy invitation around something you already like.
Belonging can begin with small repeats.
